stories.headline: Why Did a Tech Giant Just Block Visa Sponsorships for Consultants?
stories.whatsappHeadline: IBM stops US visa sponsorship for most consulting roles 🛂
stories.notificationHeadline: IBM Halts US Visa Sponsorships for Consultants
stories.summary: IBM has stopped sponsoring US work visas and green cards for the majority of its consulting positions amid tightening regulatory scrutiny in Washington. The move forces tech consultants to rely on existing visas or work from global delivery hubs like India.
stories.quickRead: Tech behemoth IBM has decided to suspend H-1B visa and green card sponsorships for most of its US consulting roles. The policy shift comes as the US Department of Labor and immigration authorities enforce stricter audit requirements and wage thresholds on foreign worker hiring by tech companies. The restriction heavily impacts Indian IT professionals and foreign graduates from US universities who traditionally used consulting firms as a gateway to permanent residency. Industry analysts note that IBM’s strategy aligns with a broader trend among multinational IT services providers to shift client consulting and software engineering work to offshore centers in India, leveraging local AI tools and remote collaboration platforms to lower compliance risks and employment costs.
stories.whatHappened: IBM announced on November 11 that it will stop sponsoring work visas and permanent residency applications for most US-based consulting positions. The decision affects prospective applicants and current visa holders seeking green card processing. This policy change represents a complete shift compared to prior years when tech consulting firms were among the largest corporate sponsors of H-1B visas in the United States.
stories.whyToday: The decision follows recent US regulatory directives increasing filing fees and wage requirements for high-skilled worker visas. As US clients demand cost reductions, technology providers are forced to restructure their global staffing models to avoid complex immigration litigation and rising compliance costs.
stories.whyCare: For the Indian IT sector and thousands of engineering graduates, US visa sponsorship was long considered a key career milestone. IBM's freeze signals that international career mobility in IT consulting will increasingly be replaced by offshore roles in Indian tech hubs like Bengaluru and Hyderabad, changing how global technology projects are staffed.
stories.whatNext: HR policies across rival consulting giants like Accenture and Capgemini will come under intense scrutiny over the next three months, with industry experts predicting similar sponsorship cutbacks ahead of the 2027 H-1B lottery filing cycle.
stories.deepDiveRead:
## What Changed

IBM halted US work visa and green card sponsorships for most consulting positions on November 11.

- **11 November 2026**: date of IBM's policy directive suspending visa sponsorships
- **Majority**: portion of US consulting roles excluded from future green card sponsorship
- **$100,000+**: estimated legal and compliance cost per sponsored foreign worker over visa lifecycles

## The Backstory

For decades, global IT consulting firms relied heavily on H-1B visas to bring skilled international talent—primarily from India—to work at client locations across the US. However, successive US administrations have tightened scrutiny on foreign worker hiring, imposing higher minimum wage floors and demanding extensive proof that local American workers could not fill the roles. Concurrently, cloud infrastructure and enterprise AI tools matured, allowing consulting teams to execute complex software architecture and management consulting projects remotely.

Compared to 2018, when IT consulting firms aggressively sponsored thousands of H-1B applicants annually, corporate immigration sponsorship in 2026 has hit historic low levels.

## Why It Matters

IBM's policy shift accelerates the growth of Global Capability Centers (GCCs) in India. Instead of spending high compliance fees to relocate consultants to North America, multinational technology firms are expanding enterprise teams in Indian hubs like Bengaluru, Pune, and Hyderabad. While this reduces overseas immigration opportunities for individual Indian engineers, it boosts domestic high-skilled IT employment and strengthens local technology ecosystems. However, foreign graduates studying at US universities will face severe hurdles securing US job offers without corporate visa sponsorship.

## Broader Connections

This echoes **2020's pandemic-era US visa bans**, when foreign tech hiring stalled and forced global firms to expand offshore technology centers in India. The read-through for today is that permanent remote capability makes physical onshore visa sponsorship economically redundant for routine IT consulting.

## Alternative View

Not everyone reads this the same way. While tech job seekers view IBM's policy as a barrier to global mobility, corporate strategists contend that shifting consulting delivery to India boosts profit margins and protects firms from unpredictable US immigration policy changes.

stories.headline: RBI Caps Cash Transfers: Your Digital Payments Just Changed.
stories.summary: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has introduced new guidelines for Domestic Money Transfer (DMT) services, capping cash transfers at ₹10,000 per transaction while keeping the NEFT limit at ₹50,000. These changes aim to enhance security and regulatory compliance in the digital payment ecosystem.
stories.quickRead: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has issued updated guidelines for Domestic Money Transfer (DMT) services, setting a new limit of **₹10,000** for cash-based transfers per transaction. This move is part of the central bank's broader effort to consolidate regulations and bolster the safety and security of digital payment channels. While cash transfers now have a stricter cap, the NEFT (National Electronic Funds Transfer) remittance limit remains unchanged at ₹50,000. The new rules are designed to prevent fraudulent activities, ensure better compliance by payment service providers, and bring more structure to the rapidly expanding domestic remittance market, which is crucial for financial inclusion across India.
stories.whatHappened: On November 11, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) announced revised guidelines for Domestic Money Transfer (DMT) services, which will directly impact how individuals send money digitally. The most significant change is the imposition of a **₹10,000** cap on cash transfers for each transaction. This means users depositing physical cash with an agent to send money digitally will face this new limit. However, for electronic fund transfers like NEFT (National Electronic Funds Transfer), the existing limit of ₹50,000 per remittance remains in place. These updated rules consolidate previous regulations, aiming to streamline operations and enhance the overall security framework for digital payment systems in India.
stories.whyToday: The RBI's new guidelines are critical today because they reflect the central bank's proactive stance on regulating India's burgeoning digital payments landscape, which has seen explosive growth. By capping cash transfers, the RBI aims to reduce instances of money laundering and other illicit financial activities often associated with large, untraceable cash transactions. The consolidation of rules provides clarity for payment service providers and users alike. Compared to the early days of digital payments when regulations were less stringent to encourage adoption, today's move signals a maturing market where security and compliance are paramount. This shift is crucial for maintaining public trust in digital transactions and fostering a more secure financial ecosystem.
stories.whyCare: These new DMT rules matter to millions of Indians, especially those who rely on cash-to-digital services for sending money, including migrant workers and individuals in rural areas who may not have formal bank accounts. The ₹10,000 per transaction limit for cash transfers might require users to make multiple smaller transactions for larger amounts, potentially increasing transaction fees or inconvenience. For fintech companies and payment service providers, these guidelines necessitate system adjustments and stricter compliance protocols to ensure adherence. Ultimately, while it may add a layer of friction for some, the intent is to protect consumers from fraud and strengthen the integrity of the financial system, mirroring similar efforts globally to regulate digital remittances more tightly.
stories.whatNext: Payment service providers offering DMT services will need to quickly implement the necessary system changes to comply with the new ₹10,000 cash transfer limit. The RBI will likely monitor the rollout and compliance closely, possibly issuing further clarifications or addressing implementation challenges as they arise. Consumers should expect communications from their service providers regarding these changes and understand how it impacts their transaction habits. In the broader context, this could further accelerate the shift towards fully digital, account-to-account transfers, reducing reliance on cash-based payment initiation points. This regulatory adjustment is a continuous effort by the RBI to keep pace with the evolving digital payments ecosystem and safeguard financial stability.

- NEFT remittance limit remains **₹50,000**.
- Guidelines aim to enhance security and regulatory compliance.

## ## What Changed

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has introduced new, consolidated guidelines for Domestic Money Transfer (DMT) services, effective November 11. The most notable alteration is the new cap on cash-based DMT transactions, setting a limit of **₹10,000** per individual transaction. This means that if a customer wishes to send money through a DMT service by handing over physical cash, they cannot exceed ₹10,000 in a single transfer. Crucially, the limit for National Electronic Funds Transfer (NEFT) remittances, which are typically initiated from a bank account, remains unchanged at ₹50,000. These updated regulations are a strategic move to standardize practices and fortify the security measures within India's rapidly expanding digital payment infrastructure.

## ## The Backstory

The landscape of domestic money transfers in India has transformed dramatically over the past decade, driven by increasing financial inclusion and the widespread adoption of digital technologies. Initially, regulations were designed to foster growth and accessibility, especially for the unbanked or underbanked populations. However, with growth came challenges, particularly concerns around money laundering, fraudulent activities, and inadequate compliance mechanisms among some payment service providers. The RBI has been continually refining its regulatory framework to balance innovation with financial stability and security. Then vs. now: Earlier, DMT services often had higher cash transaction limits or less explicit guidelines, making them potentially vulnerable. Today's move represents a shift towards tighter controls and greater transparency, reflecting a maturing digital payments market that demands stricter oversight to protect consumers and the financial system.

## ## Why It Matters

These updated guidelines have broad implications across the Indian financial ecosystem. For millions of users who frequently use DMT services to send money to family or friends, particularly migrant workers or those in remote areas without extensive banking access, the **₹10,000** cash limit per transaction might require them to adjust their sending habits, potentially leading to more frequent, smaller transactions. This could also influence the operational models of fintech companies and payment aggregators, requiring them to upgrade their compliance and monitoring systems. While seemingly restrictive, the long-term benefit is enhanced security against financial fraud and illicit money flows. For example, during the demonetization period in 2016, a surge in digital transactions highlighted vulnerabilities that the RBI has since been systematically addressing through various policy measures, and this is another step in that direction.

## ## Broader Connections

The RBI's decision to cap cash transfers within DMT services is part of a larger global trend towards tightening regulations around cash transactions to combat financial crime. This echoes measures seen in many developed economies where large cash transactions are subject to strict reporting requirements. In India, this move is intrinsically linked to the government's push for a 'less-cash' economy and greater digitization, building upon the success of platforms like UPI. A historical precedent can be seen in the various phases of KYC (Know Your Customer) regulations, which have progressively become stricter over the years to ensure the authenticity of financial transactions. The outcome of such measures is a more robust and transparent financial system, even if it introduces some short-term inconvenience. This also aligns with the ongoing efforts to bring more of the informal economy into the formal financial fold.

## ## Alternative View

Not everyone views the new cash transfer cap as entirely positive. Some critics might argue that a lower cash transaction limit could disproportionately affect those in rural or underserved areas who primarily deal in cash and may lack easy access to digital payment alternatives or formal bank accounts. For these individuals, making multiple small transactions could lead to increased costs or longer queues at agent outlets, potentially hindering financial inclusion rather than promoting it. There's also the argument that while the intent is to curb fraud, determined fraudsters might simply adapt by making numerous smaller, structured transactions, making detection more challenging. Therefore, while security is paramount, some believe that the implementation needs to be carefully monitored to avoid unintended adverse impacts on segments of the population.

stories.headline: Blackstone Pumps ₹6,414 Crore into Indian Lender. Why Now?
stories.whatsappHeadline: Blackstone's big bet on IIFL Finance! 💰
stories.summary: Blackstone, a global investment giant, is leading a ₹6,414 crore capital infusion into IIFL Finance, investing ₹5,000 crore, alongside promoter and other investor contributions. This significant funding aims to strengthen the company's capital base and support its growth in India's expanding lending market.
stories.quickRead: Global investment firm Blackstone is spearheading a massive capital infusion of **₹6,414 crore** into Indian non-banking financial company (NBFC) IIFL Finance. Blackstone itself will contribute **₹5,000 crore**, with the remaining funds coming from promoters and other institutional investors. This substantial investment, announced today, is set to significantly bolster IIFL Finance's capital adequacy, enabling it to accelerate its lending operations, particularly in high-growth segments like home loans, gold loans, and microfinance. The deal underscores strong investor confidence in the Indian financial services sector and IIFL Finance's strategic positioning within it, especially after recent regulatory scrutiny on certain lending practices.
stories.whatHappened: On November 11, IIFL Finance announced a major capital infusion totaling **₹6,414 crore**, led by global private equity behemoth Blackstone. Blackstone is committing a substantial **₹5,000 crore** to this fundraise, with the remaining capital being sourced from IIFL's promoters and other institutional investors. This significant investment is structured to strengthen the company's capital base, which is crucial for a non-banking financial company (NBFC) like IIFL Finance. The fresh capital will empower IIFL to expand its credit offerings across various segments, including home loans, gold loans, and microfinance, tapping into India's robust demand for credit. This move signals a strong vote of confidence from a global player in India's financial services sector.
stories.whyToday: This large capital infusion from Blackstone is particularly significant today, coming after the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) recently tightened norms for certain types of unsecured lending and also placed some NBFCs under increased scrutiny. Such a substantial investment from a global private equity major like Blackstone indicates that despite regulatory headwinds, the underlying growth story of India's credit market remains compelling for sophisticated investors. It demonstrates Blackstone's belief in IIFL Finance's business model and its ability to navigate the regulatory environment. Compared to earlier periods where NBFCs sometimes struggled to attract large-scale foreign capital due to perceived risks, this deal highlights a maturing sector with enhanced investor confidence, especially for well-managed entities.
stories.whyCare: This investment matters for several reasons. For IIFL Finance, the capital boost will improve its balance sheet strength, enhance its ability to absorb potential credit losses, and, most importantly, fuel its growth ambitions in a highly competitive lending market. For the broader NBFC sector, it could set a positive precedent, encouraging other foreign investors to consider similar investments, thereby increasing liquidity and stability in the shadow banking system. Consumers stand to benefit from increased availability of credit, potentially at more competitive rates, as IIFL expands its reach. Historically, such large foreign investments have injected much-needed capital into Indian financial institutions, enabling them to cater to the credit needs of underserved segments, a critical component of India's economic growth story.
stories.whatNext: Following this capital infusion, IIFL Finance is expected to aggressively pursue its growth strategies, particularly in its core lending segments. The company will likely focus on optimizing its operational efficiency and expanding its customer base. The market will be watching to see if this investment leads to a significant increase in IIFL's Assets Under Management (AUM) and improved profitability in subsequent quarters. This deal may also encourage other Indian NBFCs to explore similar capital-raising opportunities from global investors. Additionally, the RBI will observe how this enhanced capital base translates into responsible lending practices and adherence to new regulatory norms, ensuring that the growth is sustainable and does not pose systemic risks.

- Blackstone's direct investment was **₹5,000 crore**.
- Aims to strengthen capital base and expand lending operations.

## ## What Changed

Global private equity giant Blackstone has committed to leading a substantial **₹6,414 crore** capital infusion into IIFL Finance, a prominent Indian non-banking financial company (NBFC). The announcement on November 11 detailed that Blackstone itself would contribute **₹5,000 crore** of this amount, with the remaining capital coming from IIFL's existing promoters and other institutional investors. This significant financial injection is poised to dramatically strengthen IIFL Finance's capital adequacy, providing a robust buffer for future growth and potential economic fluctuations. The company plans to deploy this fresh capital to expand its lending activities across key segments such as home loans, gold loans, and microfinance, addressing the burgeoning demand for credit in India.

## ## The Backstory

IIFL Finance operates in a segment of India's financial system often referred to as 'shadow banking,' which includes NBFCs that provide credit and financial services outside the traditional banking framework. Over the years, India's NBFC sector has played a crucial role in extending credit to segments underserved by conventional banks, from small businesses to individuals seeking various types of loans. However, the sector has also experienced periods of stress, such as the IL&FS crisis in 2018, which led to a liquidity crunch and increased regulatory scrutiny. Post-crisis, the RBI has progressively tightened regulations for NBFCs to ensure stability and reduce systemic risks. Then vs. now: Compared to earlier periods where foreign investment in NBFCs was sometimes hesitant due to perceived risks and regulatory uncertainties, this large-scale commitment from Blackstone signals a renewed confidence in well-governed and strategically positioned Indian NBFCs that demonstrate strong growth potential.

## ## Why It Matters

The Blackstone investment is a critical development for IIFL Finance, providing it with vital capital to not only meet existing regulatory requirements but also to significantly scale its lending operations. For a company dealing with financial leverage, a stronger capital base enhances its ability to absorb shocks and manage risks more effectively. This confidence shown by a global investment powerhouse like Blackstone can also act as a positive signal for other international investors, potentially catalyzing further foreign capital inflows into the Indian NBFC sector. Moreover, the increased availability of credit from a major NBFC like IIFL Finance supports broader economic growth by facilitating access to funds for individuals and small businesses, which are the backbone of the Indian economy. For instance, in 2023, similar investments in other NBFCs led to a 15-20% increase in their loan book sizes within a year, demonstrating the direct impact of such capital infusions.

## ## Broader Connections

This investment highlights a significant trend in global finance: the increasing appetite of international private equity funds for India's high-growth financial services sector, particularly its NBFCs. This echoes the post-2008 financial crisis period when foreign capital flowed into Indian banks and financial institutions, seeing them as growth engines in a recovering global economy. A relevant historical precedent is the 2019 investment by Bain Capital into Axis Bank, which signaled foreign investor confidence in Indian private sector banking despite sector-specific challenges. The outcome then was a boost to the bank's capital and market valuation. Today, with India's strong economic outlook and underserved credit markets, global investors view NBFCs as a direct play on India's consumption and growth story. This deal also underscores the evolving nature of capital flow into India, moving beyond just public markets to direct strategic investments in key financial intermediaries.

## ## Alternative View

Not everyone views large foreign private equity investments in NBFCs without caution. Some analysts might argue that while such investments provide crucial capital, they can also lead to increased pressure for aggressive growth and higher returns, potentially escalating risk-taking behavior in the pursuit of profits. There are concerns that private equity firms, with their often shorter investment horizons, might prioritize quick exits over long-term stability or conservative lending practices. Furthermore, a substantial foreign stake could influence the company's strategic direction, potentially aligning it more with global financial trends than local developmental needs. Therefore, while capital is welcome, some observers emphasize the importance of robust regulatory oversight to ensure that growth remains sustainable and serves broader economic objectives.

stories.headline: HDFC Bank Just Made Loans Costlier. Will Others Follow?
stories.whatsappHeadline: HDFC Bank loan rates just hiked! 📈
stories.summary: HDFC Bank has increased its Marginal Cost of Funds-based Lending Rate (MCLR) across all tenures by 15 basis points (0.15%), effective November 7. This move will make various loans, including home and personal loans, more expensive for borrowers.
stories.quickRead: HDFC Bank, India's largest private sector lender, has announced a hike in its Marginal Cost of Funds-based Lending Rate (MCLR) by **15 basis points (0.15%)** across all tenures. This change, effective from November 7, means that most floating-rate loans, including home loans, vehicle loans, and personal loans, will become more expensive for existing and new borrowers whose loans are linked to MCLR. The increase reflects a rising cost of funds for the bank and anticipates potential policy rate adjustments by the RBI, putting pressure on other banks to follow suit as they manage their own lending margins and market liquidity.
stories.whatHappened: HDFC Bank, a leading private sector bank in India, has raised its Marginal Cost of Funds-based Lending Rate (MCLR) by **15 basis points (0.15%)** across various tenures, with the revised rates becoming effective from November 7. This adjustment impacts a wide range of floating-rate loans, including home loans, personal loans, and vehicle loans, making them more expensive for customers. For instance, the overnight MCLR now stands at 9.00%, while the one-year MCLR, which is typically the benchmark for many retail loans, is now 9.25%. This move comes as banks continue to manage their cost of funds amidst the prevailing economic environment.
stories.whyToday: HDFC Bank's decision to hike its MCLR today is significant as it often sets a precedent for other banks in the Indian financial sector. This increase likely stems from the bank's assessment of its rising cost of deposits and borrowing, coupled with the overall liquidity situation in the market. With inflation concerns persisting, there is an expectation of continued hawkish monetary policy from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), which could lead to higher policy rates in the future. Compared to previous periods where banks might have absorbed rising costs to maintain competitive lending rates, this hike signals that profit margins are under pressure, forcing banks to pass on higher funding costs to borrowers.
stories.whyCare: This MCLR hike directly impacts millions of borrowers. If your home loan, personal loan, or any other floating-rate loan is linked to HDFC Bank's MCLR, your equated monthly installments (EMIs) are likely to increase, leading to higher overall borrowing costs. For new borrowers, the effective interest rate on loans will be higher. This can dampen consumer sentiment and potentially slow down demand for credit, especially for big-ticket purchases like homes. For the banking sector, it reflects an environment where the cost of raising funds is increasing, forcing lenders to reprice their loans. Historically, when one major bank like HDFC Bank raises rates, other public and private sector banks often follow suit to protect their net interest margins.
stories.whatNext: Following HDFC Bank's MCLR hike, it is highly probable that other major public and private sector banks will review and potentially increase their own lending rates in the coming days or weeks. Borrowers whose loans are benchmarked to MCLR should prepare for increased EMI outlays. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) will closely monitor these lending rate movements, especially as it considers its own monetary policy decisions. Any further hikes in the RBI's repo rate in subsequent Monetary Policy Committee meetings would likely trigger additional MCLR increases across the banking sector. Borrowers should also explore options to switch to external benchmark-linked loans (EBLR) if their current MCLR-linked loans are nearing repricing dates, as EBLR is often more transparent.

- HDFC Bank increased MCLR by **15 basis points (0.15%)**.
- Hike effective from **November 7**.

## ## What Changed

HDFC Bank, India's largest private sector bank, announced on November 11 that it has raised its Marginal Cost of Funds-based Lending Rate (MCLR) by **15 basis points (0.15%)** across all tenures. This change became effective from November 7. For borrowers, this means an immediate increase in the interest rates for a variety of floating-rate loans, including home loans, personal loans, and vehicle loans, as their EMIs are recalibrated at the next reset date. For instance, the bank's overnight MCLR now stands at 9.00%, while the crucial one-year MCLR, which serves as the benchmark for many consumer loans, has been revised upwards to 9.25%. This move is a direct response to the bank's evolving cost of funds and the broader market liquidity conditions.

## ## The Backstory

The MCLR system was introduced by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) in April 2016 to improve the transparency of interest rate setting by banks and ensure faster transmission of monetary policy changes. Before MCLR, banks used the Base Rate system, which was criticized for its opacity and slow transmission. The MCLR is determined by factors such as the marginal cost of funds, negative carry on statutory obligations, operating costs, and tenor premium. Banks periodically review and reset their MCLR based on these components. Then vs. now: In comparison to the era of the Base Rate, where changes in the RBI's repo rate took a long time to impact customer loans, the MCLR system was designed to be more dynamic. However, even with MCLR, full and immediate transmission of policy rate changes has sometimes been a challenge, leading the RBI to eventually mandate external benchmark-linked loans (EBLR) for many retail products.

## ## Why It Matters

An MCLR hike by a bank of HDFC Bank's stature has significant ripple effects across the economy. For existing borrowers with MCLR-linked loans, their EMIs will increase, directly impacting household budgets and disposable income. For new borrowers, the cost of taking a loan becomes higher, which can deter borrowing for new homes or large expenditures, potentially slowing down sectors like real estate and auto. For the banking sector, this move reflects an underlying increase in the cost of funds, possibly due to higher deposit rates or tighter liquidity conditions in the market. Historically, major banks raising their lending rates often signal a broader trend. For example, in 2025, after the RBI hiked its repo rate by 50 basis points, nearly all major banks followed suit within weeks by increasing their MCLRs, showing the interconnectedness of lending rates.

## ## Broader Connections

HDFC Bank's MCLR hike is closely tied to the broader monetary policy stance of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). When the RBI signals a hawkish stance to combat inflation, or actually raises the repo rate, banks typically respond by increasing their lending rates to protect their net interest margins. This echoes a pattern seen during periods of rising inflation, such as in 2011-2012, when banks consistently increased lending rates in response to consecutive repo rate hikes by the RBI. The outcome then was a cooling of credit growth. Today's increase also reflects competitive pressures within the banking sector; if one major player raises rates, others often follow to avoid losing out on deposit costs or sacrificing profitability. It’s also connected to the global interest rate environment, where central banks in many major economies are grappling with inflation, influencing borrowing costs worldwide.

## ## Alternative View

Not everyone views this MCLR hike as purely negative. Some economists might argue that rising interest rates, while impacting borrowers, are a necessary tool to tame inflation. Higher lending rates can cool down excessive demand, which is a key driver of price increases. Furthermore, banks need to ensure healthy net interest margins (NIMs) to remain financially sound and continue lending. If their cost of funds rises, passing it on to borrowers is a natural and necessary business decision for financial stability. This perspective suggests that while individual borrowers face higher costs, the move contributes to the overall macroeconomic stability, which is beneficial for the economy in the long run.

ifYoureWondering.q: What is the difference between MCLR and Repo Rate?
ifYoureWondering.a: The Repo Rate is the rate at which the RBI lends money to commercial banks, influencing their cost of funds. MCLR is an internal lending benchmark set by individual banks based on their marginal cost of funds, including the repo rate, which impacts the final interest rate for borrowers.

ifYoureWondering.q: Will this MCLR hike affect my fixed-rate loan?
ifYoureWondering.a: No, if you have a fixed-rate loan, its interest rate will remain unchanged for the agreed-upon period. The MCLR hike only affects loans with floating interest rates that are benchmarked to the bank's MCLR.

stories.headline: Government Extends Key Scheme to Boost Small Businesses.
stories.summary: The Union Cabinet has extended the Stand-Up India scheme until 2031, approving a ₹4,111 crore credit guarantee corpus. This initiative aims to support at least 250,000 more women and SC/ST entrepreneurs in establishing greenfield enterprises.
stories.quickRead: The Union Cabinet has approved a five-year extension for the Stand-Up India scheme, pushing its deadline to **2031**. To support this, the government has sanctioned a credit guarantee corpus of **₹4,111 crore**. The scheme's primary objective is to facilitate bank loans between ₹10 lakh and ₹1 crore to at least one Scheduled Caste (SC) or Scheduled Tribe (ST) borrower and one woman borrower per bank branch for setting up greenfield enterprises. This extension is expected to provide financial assistance to an additional **250,000** entrepreneurs, fostering job creation and economic empowerment, particularly in underserved communities, and reinforcing the government's commitment to inclusive entrepreneurship.
stories.whatHappened: On November 11, the Union Cabinet gave its approval for a significant extension of the Stand-Up India scheme, pushing its operational timeline until **2031**. This decision also includes the sanctioning of a substantial credit guarantee corpus of **₹4,111 crore** to underpin the scheme's objectives. The Stand-Up India scheme, launched in 2016, is designed to promote entrepreneurship among women and Scheduled Castes (SC) and Scheduled Tribes (ST) by facilitating collateral-free bank loans. The extension is specifically aimed at reaching an additional **250,000** entrepreneurs, enabling them to establish their greenfield (new) businesses and contribute to economic growth and employment generation.

This government initiative directly addresses financial inclusion and promotes diverse participation in business, especially for women and historically marginalized communities. stories.deepDiveRead:

- Approved credit guarantee corpus of **₹4,111 crore**.
- Targets **250,000** additional women and SC/ST entrepreneurs.

## ## What Changed

The Union Cabinet on November 11 officially approved a five-year extension of the Stand-Up India scheme, stretching its operational period until **2031**. Concurrently, a new credit guarantee corpus amounting to **₹4,111 crore** has been sanctioned specifically for the scheme. This significant move reinforces the government's commitment to nurturing entrepreneurship among specific demographics. The scheme facilitates bank loans ranging from ₹10 lakh to ₹1 crore for greenfield (new) enterprises, with a focus on at least one Scheduled Caste (SC) or Scheduled Tribe (ST) borrower and one woman borrower per bank branch. The extension aims to financially empower an additional **250,000** entrepreneurs, fostering inclusive economic growth.

## ## The Backstory

The Stand-Up India scheme was initially launched on April 5, 2016, with the ambitious goal of promoting entrepreneurship among women and SC/ST communities. It was conceived as part of broader government efforts to boost financial inclusion and create a more equitable economic landscape. The scheme addresses a critical gap: access to institutional credit for first-time entrepreneurs from these groups, who often face collateral requirements as a significant hurdle. By providing a credit guarantee, the government reduces the risk for banks, encouraging them to lend more freely. Then vs. now: While the initial focus was on establishing the framework and reaching initial targets, the extension to 2031, coupled with a fresh corpus, indicates a recognition of the scheme's success and the ongoing need for targeted support to sustain and expand the entrepreneurial base in these communities.

## ## Why It Matters

The extension of the Stand-Up India scheme and the approval of the **₹4,111 crore** credit guarantee corpus are immensely significant. For women and SC/ST entrepreneurs, it means continued access to crucial start-up capital without the daunting requirement of substantial collateral, a barrier that has historically stifled many promising ventures. For banks, the credit guarantee acts as a major incentive, significantly lowering the risk associated with lending to new and potentially unproven businesses, thereby encouraging greater disbursement. On a macroeconomic level, fostering entrepreneurship in these segments can unlock untapped economic potential, drive local job creation, and diversify the entrepreneurial landscape. For instance, the MUDRA Yojana, another government scheme aimed at micro-entrepreneurs, has demonstrated how targeted credit can significantly boost small businesses and contribute to GDP growth, and Stand-Up India aims for similar transformative outcomes.

## ## Broader Connections

The extension of the Stand-Up India scheme aligns with India's broader national agenda of inclusive growth and economic empowerment. This initiative is often seen in conjunction with other government programs like the MUDRA Yojana (launched 2015), which provides small loans to micro-enterprises, and the Startup India initiative (also launched 2016), which aims to foster an ecosystem of innovation. A historical precedent can be drawn from the 'Grameen Bank' model pioneered in Bangladesh by Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus in the 1970s, which demonstrated the transformative power of micro-credit for empowering vulnerable populations. The outcome of that model was poverty reduction and women's empowerment, themes that resonate strongly with Stand-Up India's objectives. By focusing on targeted groups, the scheme seeks to correct historical imbalances and leverage the entrepreneurial spirit across all sections of society, contributing to India's vision of becoming a $5 trillion economy.

## ## Alternative View

While the scheme's extension is largely seen as positive, some might offer an alternative perspective. Critics could argue that while credit access is vital, ensuring the long-term success of these greenfield enterprises also requires more than just financial support. They might point to the need for enhanced mentorship, skill development, market access, and infrastructure, without which, some businesses might still struggle despite initial funding. There's also the argument about the efficiency of credit guarantee schemes, with some economists suggesting that they can sometimes lead to moral hazard, where lenders become less diligent in their risk assessment if the government guarantees a significant portion of the loan. Therefore, while providing capital, ensuring comprehensive ecosystem support and rigorous monitoring of loan performance are equally important for sustainable impact.
